adjudications.reason: The amendment adds the Ombudsman for Public Complaints against Judges, alongside the committee chair, to those who may propose a judge's removal under s. 7(4). It therefore engages an independent judiciary, with the removal of judges as principal subject, and None is unavailable because the seq 19 and 31 rulings reserve None for a text that engages no value. Widening the routes by which removal can be set in motion lessens judges' security of tenure; that is a contradiction of the value rather than a rearrangement of it, and nothing in the text entrenches it. It is limited, not sharp, because the decision stays with the Judges' Selection Committee under its unchanged decision rule. I adopt Coder A's reading; Coder B's own note concedes Limited if an added initiator of removal counts as a contradiction, and I hold that it does.

adjudications.support: s. 7(4): a proposal to end a judge's tenure may now also come from the Ombudsman for Public Complaints against Judges; decision rule unchanged.
adjudications.reason: The principal subject is the removal of judges, and the one axis engaged is judicial independence. On the item 1 ruling the text narrows that independence by adding an initiator of removal, and the definition codes such a narrowing Illiberal however marginal. Neutral is for texts that engage none of the axes, and changing who may set a judge's removal in motion is not procedural housekeeping, even though the decision rule is unchanged; coding Neutral would also contradict the Limited finding on the same text, so I adopt Coder A's value.

adjudications.reason: Sections 1 and 2 exempt faction splits that meet the Elections Law conditions from the bar in ss. 5(b1) and 34(b) on appointing a member who left his faction as minister or deputy minister, and s. 3 extends the exemption to splits made before commencement; the principal subject is that eligibility rule. The bar belongs to the anti-defection regime that the ruling on Basic Law: The Knesset (Amendment No. 12) found to engage free and equal elections and rule of law, but unlike s. 6A it does not touch candidacy: its function is to stop executive office being the reward for leaving one's faction, the integrity concern that ruling treated as rule of law, so None is unavailable, rule of law is the principal value and free and equal elections is secondary. Narrowing that safeguard, and doing so retroactively for members whose position was already fixed, contradicts rule of law, as loosening a check did in the 2013 ruling, and the contradiction is limited because individual defection stays barred and only statutory splits are exempt. I adopt Coder A's value with a different principal value, deciding from the text alone.

adjudications.support: s. 5(b): על אף האמור בסעיף 36א לחוק–יסוד: הכנסת, היום הקובע לגבי חוק התקציב הדו–שנתי לשנים 2015 ו–2016 יהיה ... (19 בנובמבר 2015)

On the seq 101 reading, a specific interest of the government is one it holds for itself, including its tenure. Section 5, whose marginal note names the Knesset's dissolution for failure to adopt this budget law, sets s. 36A aside and moves the day on which failure to pass this government's 2015-2016 budget would dissolve the Knesset and bring early elections, from no later than about 22 August 2015 (100 days from formation under s. 36A(b)) to 19 November 2015; that addresses the government's tenure rather than the public end of an appropriation, a text difference the seq 101 reading makes relevant, since seqs 101 to 118 and the 2023 enactment set crisis spending or reporting dates and leave the dissolution rule alone. The explanatory notes (Government Bills 916, p. 590) have no archive capture, so I code from the text and adopt Coder A's value.

adjudications.reason: The text governs when the government must bring its budget and when budget failure dissolves the Knesset, so it engages separation of powers as principal subject, and on the seq 19 and 31 reading None is unavailable. As in the ruling on the 2013 amendment (Amendment No. 2), s. 5(b) sets s. 36A aside and fixes the determining day at 19 November 2015, nearly three months after the s. 36A(b) date; this lengthens the time the government may run on a continuing budget without a budget law, which contradicts the value. The contradiction is limited because it covers one budget and a date the Knesset itself fixed, and s. 5(a) (the Finance Committee sets the tabling date) and the duty to table a 2017-2018 plan are entrenching elements that the precedence rule subordinates. I adopt Coder A's value; Coder A's free-elections axis is not needed for it, and 'fiscal housekeeping' is a ground for Neutral direction, not for a None tier.

adjudications.support: Penal Law s. 2(b), identical before and after the repeal: "תקנות שבהן נקבעו עבירות ועונשים טעונות אישור ועדה של הכנסת"
adjudications.reason: The check is the requirement that a Knesset committee approve ministerial regulations creating criminal offences before they take effect. The enactment deletes s. 21A from the Basic Law, but s. 21A(b) itself preserved other laws on regulations, and Penal Law s. 2(b) imposes the same approval requirement without s. 21A's 45-day deemed-approval proviso; it is marked as amended in 1994 and is identical in the Wikisource revisions of 2 July and 17 August 2016. The repeal therefore neither removes the check nor renders it inoperative, so the definition's first condition fails whatever the enactment itself provides, and an alternative mechanism exists in ordinary law. I adopt Coder A's value but correct its dating: the Penal Law rule predates the repeal rather than accompanying it.

adjudications.support: Raises May-December crisis shares; business grants NIS 9bn to 16bn; ministries 11bn to 14bn; NII repayment 16.1bn to 14.6bn; para. (2a) update due 15.7.2020.
adjudications.reason: The seq 101 ruling held that authority to spend in 2020 without a budget law, beyond the one-twelfth rule, contradicts separation of powers to a limited extent, and the seq 105 and 109 rulings held that amendments resetting the monthly crisis shares and plan amounts measure that authority and are Limited, whatever the amounts. This text does the same: it raises the May-December shares and most plan components and lowers two items, so it differs from seqs 105 and 109 only in amount. The new para. (2a) duty to submit an updated plan to the Finance Committee by 15 July 2020, and the Finance Committee condition on the added NIS 500 million business grant, are entrenching elements that the precedence rule subordinates, so Coder A's Entrenches fails, and Coder B's None fails because the text engages a value. Limited, departing from both coders so that like cases are decided alike.

adjudications.support: s. 2 (to 31.12.2021 or the 2021 budget law): לשם מימון ההוצאות הדרושות להתמודדות עם המשבר ... סכום שלא יעלה על 52.3 מיליארד שקלים חדשים
adjudications.reason: Section 2 lets the government spend up to NIS 52.3 billion in 2021 for the coronavirus crisis, outside any budget law and beyond the one-twelfth continuing budget. That is the same authority the seq 101 ruling held contradicts separation of powers to a limited extent, and the tension Coder A's own note records. The Knesset-fixed sums and headings, the stated sole purpose, the one-year term and the new s. 3B(b1) duty to lay the spending plan before the government and submit it to the Finance Committee are the bounds and entrenching elements that ruling treated as keeping the contradiction limited and as subordinated by precedence, so Entrenches fails; and the permanent s. 3B changes, including indexing the monthly one-twelfth to population growth, also concern spending without a budget law, so the text engages a value and None fails. Limited, departing from both coders, consistent with seqs 101, 105 and 109.

interpretive_rulings.question: Q1
interpretive_rulings.reading_adopted: Item 4 covers a single-instance clause that by its own terms applies only to the government in office at commencement and, for that government's term, exempts it from a limit the new rule imposes on its own organs; the item is not confined to clauses that end a measure.
interpretive_rulings.reason: Section 2 applies new s. 27(b)-(c) to 'the government serving on the day of commencement', except the limit on the size of the ministerial committee for national security, while s. 27(b) binds every government from its formation; so the exemption is confined by its own terms to the sitting government and its term, as the ruling on Basic Law: The Knesset (Amendment No. 12) requires, and the committee's added members are fixed by that government's own decision. The alteration, freedom from the cap, belongs to that government alone, since each successor is bound from formation; 'single-instance' covers a clause applying to one government, so I reject the narrower reading that would confine item 4 to clauses ending a measure. Government: the 24th government under Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir (in office 11.6.1990 to 13.7.1992, Knesset government record, archive capture 26.6.2004); matter: the size of its ministerial committee for national security; fact: s. 2 of the enactment, passed 5.2.1991. Source: ס״ח 1344, p. 86 (15.2.1991), gazette text https://web.archive.org/web/20220618023516/https://fs.knesset.gov.il/12/law/12_lsr_210831.pdf (capture 18.6.2022).

interpretive_rulings.question: Q2
interpretive_rulings.reading_adopted: Item 1 reaches a general provision only where it has direct legal effect on the question pending before the court and only the sitting person or government is party to it; a prospective repeal tied to a pending case only by a committee chair's stated wish rests on motive.
interpretive_rulings.reason: The repeal has no transitional, application or retroactivity clause, so it does not decide the question the record says was pending: whether fisheries regulations had already been deemed approved under the s. 21A proviso before 2 August 2016. Nor does the record identify the parties or show the government relying on deemed approval (Protocol 156 says the proviso was not applied in practice), and the repeal binds every minister alike, while the committee-approval requirement continues for every government under Penal Law s. 2(b) (item 8). The only link to the case is the chair's stated wish that the court 'understand the direction', which is motive and is excluded. I looked for direct legal effect in the enactment's text, in s. 21A and Penal Law s. 2 as they stood, and in the protocols the reader cites, and did not search court records.

interpretive_rulings.question: Q3
interpretive_rulings.reading_adopted: Item 4 is not met by a provision keyed to a budget year or a named budget, which like a Knesset's term covers whichever government holds office then, so partial sharing defeats it; item 3 is met where the enactment itself moves a fixed deadline then running against the sitting government, and the unshared alteration is the move of that deadline, which a successor operating under the new date does not share.
interpretive_rulings.reason: Section 2 sets s. 36A aside and fixes the determining day for the 2009-2010 budget at 107 days from the government's formation. Under s. 36A(b) as then in force (he.wikisource revision 242370, 22.10.2008) the determining day was the later of three months into the fiscal year or 45 days from formation, so for the 32nd government, formed 31.3.2009 (Knesset government record, archive capture 1.1.2011), the deadline moved from about 15 May to about 16 July 2009, consistent with the 45-day deadline the reader's pre-passage press reported; that date was computed from the sitting government's formation, and its lapse would dissolve the Knesset and bring elections ending the government's term, so it bound that government, only its deadline was moved, and s. 1(a)(2) also fixes its tabling date at 16 June 2009. Item 4 is not met, since the provisions are keyed to the 2009-2010 budget rather than to the government's own measure or term. Yes under item 3: the 32nd government; matter: the determining day for its budget; fact: s. 2, dated 7.4.2009; source: ס״ח 2196, 7.4.2009, p. 134 (https://web.archive.org/web/2/https://fs.knesset.gov.il/18/law/18_lsr_301021.pdf).
